[The Auspicious Invocation and the Subject Matter] Bow down to Vāṇī,
who dwells within the lotus-like mouth of the Son of the Supreme Person (Nārāyaṇa).
The wise, who are like bees, lick the moonlight of the Doctrine (Jina-śāsana).
(GāRaKo 1) Having taken the various jewels that are the aphorisms from the ocean of the words of the wise, this treasury of verses has been fashioned.
(GāRaKo 2)
1. Now, the Praise of the Jina] First of all, pay homage to the first Jina, who is beautiful with the rays of light from the jewels in his crown.
His lotus-feet are the storehouse for the seeds of the tree of liberation that sprouts forth;
even though he has attained another kalpa, they never cease to be the ornament of his mouth. (GāRaKō.3)
The moon reaches that abode of the lotus-clan; bow down to the Jina Vīra.
2. Now, the praise of Brahmā]
Bow down to Him who is free from the stain of the three-fold impurity, in whose lotus-like abode the multitude of worlds, having undertaken the task of creation, dwells like a swarm of bees;
first, bow to the white lotus-pond that is the source of the lotuses.
Like a lotus stalk placed within the deep cavity of Hari’s navel, he is the Self-Existent One. — GāRaKō.6 [3.
Now, the Praise of Viṣṇu]
Bow down to Hari, who, while supporting the earth, is fanned by the wind stirred by the jewel-mirrors on the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa, and who beholds the herd of boars and other creatures.
Bow down to him upon whose chest the face of Lakṣmī is reflected in the Kaustubha gem. (GāRakō. 7)
The orb of the moon is seen devoid of its luster within the solar disc.
May the line of bees following the lotuses in the hidden navel-lake of Lakṣmī protect you—she who, in her role as the illusory wife of Viṣṇu, is like a forest of hair. (GāRaKō. 8–9)
Victory to Hari, who, in this circle of the world filled with water shimmering like the orb of the autumn moon, rests amidst the playful grace of the deer’s shadow.
[4. 4. Now, the Praise of Maheśvara:

We bow to him upon whose head the crescent of the moon shines, appearing like a bracelet broken by a mountain woman angry during a lovers' quarrel, caught in the coils of his flowing matted locks. (Gāthā-ratnākara 11)

Bow down to Rudra, who possesses a body that delights the eleven [faces], and whose reflection is fixed upon the tips of the feet of Gaurī as she playfully bends in devotion— reflected in his ten mirror-like nails.
Worship him who bears the playful burden of the mass of matted hair.
Worship the moon, which has its remaining luster surpassed by the face of Gauri, as if it were the moon itself;

worship the twilight-water-offering with joined palms, in which the reflection of Gauri’s moon-like face—reddened by her husband’s anger—is captured, appearing like a lotus held for worship. (GāRaKō. 13–14)
O Nanda, the flow of the Sarasvatī of the wise poets— whose course is self-directed, whose value is great due to its weight of filling the pure quarters, and whose expansion is checked by the ocean—
has had its essence seized by the foremost of poets from day one throughout the entire cycle of existence.
Even today, the movement of his speech triumphs like an unsealed seal. (GāRaKo.
16) Bow to the multitude of toe-nails on Bhāratī’s feet, which reflect the eyes of the great lord of poets as he bows down, appearing like an offering of blue lotuses. (GāRaKo. 17)
I bow to that Goddess Bhāratī, in whose mirror-like toenails the poets, as they prostrate themselves, clearly become multivocal at that very moment. (GāRakō.

[6.6. Now, the Praise of Poetry: Indeed, a poetic narrative full of aesthetic flavor delights the mind of someone; yet not all trees blossom at the touch of the feet of a beautiful young woman. (GāRaKo. 19)
When Prakrit poetry—playful, sweet-syllabled, beloved by young women, and full of erotic charm—is present, who would be able to recite Sanskrit?
To recite and compose Prakrit poetry, as well as the blossoms of the *kujjaya* tree, [is not for everyone]. (GāRaKō. 20)
Even today, many do not know how to clarify what has been obscured.
(GāRaKō.21) When the ocean of the poets' hearts is churned by the churning-stick of the wish-fulfilling tree of thought, jewels of poetry emerge. (GāRaKō.22)
What is the use of that poetry or that love which does not cause one’s head to shake— [a head] whose cloak of dense horripilation is incessant and which produces joy in the minds of people?
Victorious be those poets, from whose feet the world of scholars draws sustenance, just as [beings] draw it from the ocean!
In this world, wise men bring about the exaltation of the fortunate;
they delight the hearts of the virtuous and darken the faces of the wicked—even with poetry that is merely pleasant to hear. Homage to those great poets! (GāRaKō.24–25)
The heart is consumed by the verses of the female bards—even though they are adorned, enchanting, and full of mutual passion—as they approach;
that which is composed by those ignorant of *chandas* (prosody) is not beautiful. (Gāthākośa 26)
Is it not the case that verse is service, or rather, that even verse is service? Indeed, there are utterances of half-syllables and truly playful half-smiles. (GāRaKo 27) [p. 4]
Even the side-long glances of a woman are not understood without verses.
(GāRaKō.28) Just as a mango tree perishes and becomes lusterless through the gnawing of its bark, so too does Prakrit poetry and love fade away like a flickering flame. (GāRaKō.29)
Now, the Departure for the Ocean] The ocean of jewels, though filled incessantly with gems, indeed feels no pride.
The gaze of an elephant, intoxicated by rut, is indeed comparable to a pearl;
yet the ocean does not become insignificant because of the jewels it has produced. Nevertheless, like the moon, such jewels in the ocean are rare. (GāRaKo 30–31)
Even if he were somehow unable to satisfy [his desire] while bestowing upon the gods a multitude of jewels,
there would still be no comparison for the ocean of Manmatha even in the three worlds. The ocean,
though scorched by the submarine fire, remains cool with the rays of the moon.
Those waves of yours—
which are difficult to perceive as they flow, white with thick foam, and terrifying with the roar of crocodiles—
where have they gone now that the ocean has been rendered motionless? (GāRaKō.33–34)
O Ocean, you who always carry within your belly fire and water, nectar and poison, as well as Kṛṣṇa and the Ānavas—your greatness alone is unprecedented.
Though possessing the jewel of nectar at your command, you do not create an immortal body for the world. (Gāthākośa 35)
O Lord of Rivers, you do not feel shame at your surging waves! (GāRakō.
36) On the other hand, the surface of the earth is filled with floods of pus;
yet the ocean endures once more the blows from the tails of massive fish. (GāRakō. 37)
Though she is forbidden again and again, the Revā does not abandon the ocean;

or rather, when one's beloved is entirely salty, who is able to be angry? (Gāthākośa 38) Even though the submarine fire is situated within his heart, he remains a mass of water for the family of poison.
Behold the power of its fame: it is called the "Ocean of Jewels.
Lakṣmī is its daughter, Hari its son-in-law, and Gaṅgā its devoted wife.
O, how wonderful is the family of the Moon, the source of nectar!
Indeed, that is the majesty of the saltiness [of the ocean], that even rivers—though they consist of cruel creatures and are dull by nature—fall of their own accord into the sea. (GāRaKō. 40–41)
Just as the rivers pour forth water, so the ocean becomes exhausted;
how can great beings desire the power of women?
Though being filled with waters by the clouds, the ocean grows thin.
Even when those who have risen to great heights fall, it is a descent for the noble. (GāRaKo 43) O Ocean!
You did not dry up, nor did you sink to the bottom; why then did you not burst asunder? For even the birds perched upon your shores passed away from thirst. (GāRaKo 44)
Without Lakṣmī, the depth of the ocean remains exactly as it was;
yet without him, whose house does that Lakṣmī not roam? (GāRaKo.
45) It is the nature of the great to accept those who are destitute, regardless of any underlying motive.
Even on a stone slab at the foot of a mountain, the ocean maintains its nature.
[8. Now begins the section on the Submarine Fire (Vaḍavānala):]
O Khavanta! O Vaḍavānala! Homage to you, whose waters are not drunk by living beings and are not even tasted by flocks of birds. [GāRaKo.
47] Let the Vaḍavā fire dry up the water of the ocean, or let it not dry it up at all.

What is not already sufficient by the very fact that the fire attains [extinction] in water? (GāRaKo 48) How can that thirst of the submarine fire be quenched by the myriads of rivers, when it has not been moistened even by the waves of the ocean, which plunge into the depths of the netherworld? (GāRaKo 49)
What is equal to the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*) among other radiant things?
It is that whose mass of flames consumes even the ocean as its fuel.
[GāRaKo 50] Between the ocean and the submarine fire, which are intent upon burning and drying each other respectively—
As long as there is agitation, so long does the world of living beings live happily. (GāRaKō.
51) The treasure of jewels is for those giving among the ranks of men who are either supreme or base; but for those seeking it, it is like the submarine fire. (GāRaKō. 52)
6] ———————————————————————— [9. Now begins the section on the Play of Kṛṣṇa]

O Kṛṣṇa! Even if there were not a single virtue among the cowherd girls, even so, you should not be filled with pride on account of their upright character. Indeed, though Keśava has lifted the burden of the world, he was [overwhelmed] by the weight of Rādhā’s anger.
Who would not be softened by love, weighed down as if by a petal of a blue lotus? (GāRaKō.54) Why are you emaciated, O Keśava? Why, O fool, have you not gathered wealth?
For one who merely consumes what has been provided, how can there be any satisfaction of the mind? (GāRaKō.55)
"O Kṛṣṇa! It is true that this female serpent is indeed more venomous than a male snake;
for even though you have bowed down in submission, she has made you reel. Even in the dark water, Kṛṣṇa was pointed out by the jewels on the hoods of the serpents. (GāRakō 56)
Even those born of his own body fail him when his divine power turns away. (GāRaKō.
57) Many celestial and human women arise and pass away repeatedly in the ocean;
that is Lakṣmī, by whom the chest of Kṛṣṇa is adorned. (GāRaKō. 58)
Even though he has departed from the ocean, Murāri’s heart has been won over by Kuṣṭha;
yet we do not know what else has been placed in that spot by him.
That is heaven, that is Lakṣmī, those are the garments, and those are the ornaments.
The deer, deprived of Rāhu’s head, thumps its chest again and again.

(GāRaKo 60) What indeed must be done as a counter-measure by that Lakṣmī of Kṛṣṇa, who, though she has not been released from his heart, still follows him even while he is engaged with another? (GāRaKo 61)
[10. Now begins the description of the city:
There, the moonstone pillars were marked by the reflection of the moon, and the crystal palaces were made of sunstones.
In the conjunction of the sun and moon, it dries up the waters of the ocean and nourishes them [again].
(GāRaKo 62) Where the crystal palace, with its emerald peaks reflecting the waters of the ocean, shines like Viṣṇu reclining upon his serpent-bed at the end of the cosmic ocean. (GāRaKo 63)
Where, at night, the celestial abodes become like shower-houses due to the stone statues of Śiva’s consort, which shimmer incessantly with the rays of moonlight;
where, day after day, one beholds Gaurī and Maheśvara in their radiant splendor.
Where even the white palace walls, like the Himalayas,
bear the reflection of one's own self upon their jeweled surfaces. (GāRakō.65)
Guileless young women become angry with their lovers when they suspect them of infidelity. (GāRaKo.
66) Where the reflections of the young women’s feet fall upon the floor made of clear crystal, innocent bees mistake them for water-lilies shimmering in the water and suck at them. (GāRaKo. 67)

Where fields are devoid of crops and no noble men are seen, O best of Brahmins, there are only those eager to take up seats of kusa grass. The excellent halls are crowded with women and filled with abundant leaves.
Wherein the palaces shine within and the groves without;
there, upon a floor of sapphire, a new bride, mistaking her own reflection for a lotus, stretches out her hand toward it to seize it. (Gāthā-ratnākara 69–70)
In that place, swans—eager for lotus stalks—long for the bracelets of moonlight reflected upon the tresses of beloved women sleeping at the head of their beds.
(GāRaKō. 71)
[11. Now, the section on good people:

Good people do not desire even a fragment of this world; like a jewel-lamp, they do not become even slightly soiled by their own impurities when the particular state of their condition is unknown. (GāRaKō. 72)
The moon dispels the darkness and even vomits it up in the guise of soot;
likewise, others who are pure by nature do not harbor impurity in their hearts. From the mouth of a good person, even if they are turbid with intense anger, how could there be anything unpleasant?
Even within the mouth of Rāhu, the rays of the moon surely emit only nectar.
(GāRaKō.74) A slanderer is a fire of extreme heat that instantly consumes thousands of affections;
a true friend, however, is a mild fire that does not consume even a single affection. (GāRaKō.75)
How can even a stainless crystal, whose nature is altered by its environment, serve as a comparison for the heart of a virtuous person, which remains of a single, uniform character? (GāRaKō.
76) Even without speaking, the ultimate disposition of noble men is known through their deeds.
What do jewels say, that they are seized by the thousands?
A true friend, though unseen, kills like an arrow—fixed in the heart, taking the side of the afflicted, endowed with virtue, and resolute. (Gāthākośa 77–78)
The noble deeds of these two great-souled men shine forth, as they bestow millions of gifts with both hands raised high in generosity. (GāRakō. 79)
The prosperity of virtuous men— who are like trees that endure those who are uprooted, arrogant, and the abodes of many flocks of birds— bears fruit only as service to others.
May he be victorious by whom even the wicked were fashioned here in this world as "good people" [for their sake].
Even the rays of the moon do not reach their full splendor without him. (GāRaKō.
81) Wherever virtuous men flourish and dwell even for a moment, that very age in which they were born is truly brought to its ultimate perfection. (GāRaKō. 82)
Even for those who have ended their quarrels, the secrets shared with virtuous friends—which never escaped from their hearts—burn like fire at the end of their lifespan.
(GāRaKo 83) They are eaten whole, "crunch" (ṭasa), not by being broken apart; they are drunk, not by sipping (ghuṇṭehiṃ).
Nevertheless, even so, they bring satisfaction through their conversation to virtuous people. (GāRaKō.
84) Not even slightly can the thread strung with pearls be perceived in necklaces; it is no wonder that even those of good qualities are obscured by those whose virtues are superior. (GāRaKō. 85)
In what region do virtuous men still exist, unswallowed by the jaws of the Kali age?
Even today, Fortune has preserved them like a seed within a hollowed-out joint.
For even the crookedness of the moon, which had resorted to him as he was pacifying his host of rays— [GāRaKo. 86]
Noble men are devoted with joined palms to those possessing supernatural powers, but not to those who have fallen from their state.
(GāRaKō.87) Rare indeed are those who, having rendered service, depart without looking back like rain-clouds;
they waste away in separation, like the flow of a river. (GāRaKō.88)
There are indeed many pure pearls produced in the ocean of jewels,
yet they do not possess that fame in the world which was attained by the pearl born from the five-faced one (the conch).
[GāRaKō.89] Of those that are cut, dried up, scorched, or filled with holes...

Even for those whose faces have been defiled by me, the sound of their noble lineage has become a source of happiness in my heart; yet it has neither spread abroad nor been made manifest to the world. Indeed, the tree of resolve belonging to great men is recognized only by its fruits. (GāRaKo 90–91)

Indeed, Fortune does not clearly abide upon the head of a bee, nor upon a cluster of lotuses, nor even upon the milk-ocean; rather, she clearly resides in the tree of resolve of virtuous men. (GāRaKo.
Association with the virtuous bestows some measure of goodness even upon those who are wicked by nature;
like collyrium mixed with soot, it brings beauty even to the eye of one who is worn out.
For those who are pure through true conduct, their splendors increase even when they are intent on falsehood. (Gāthākośa 93)
The ascent of pearls with holes onto the chest of a king—what is the point of this? Does the heaviness of the courtyard of the sky diminish by that much?
It has not been equaled by the weight of even a virtuous person’s heart. (GāRaKō.94–95)
Now, the section on wicked people:
A good person is like frost; when heated, it melts, but it does not burn.
Likewise, the fire of affection for the wicked burns even more intensely. (GāRaKo.
96) No one is able to practice goodness if they are inwardly impure;
even though he bears it upon his head, the moon remains crooked, like that of Hara. (GāRaKo. 97)
Those men who, being devoid of virtue, carry themselves with pride on account of their lineage are fools;
tell me, what can a bow do, even if it is produced from a noble species of wood, if it lacks a string? Even those who are great appear small when reflected in mirrors. (GāRaKo 98)
It is only fitting that ashes should be poured into the mouth of such a person. (GāRaKō.
99) Even for men of noble birth, lineage is not the cause of modesty; does not poison kill, even though it is a brother to the nectar of the moon? (GāRaKō. 100)
Just as gold, so too does the iron arrow weigh the same on the scale;
or rather, how can there be an investigation of merits and faults for those who are devoid of letters? O double-faced one!
O letterless one! O iron-made one! O arrow! How much more shall we say?
You did not go to the underworld while weighing gold against gunja berries. (GāRaKō.
102) Like a lamp that consumes its oil, a wicked person whose virtues have been destroyed and whose sole nature is manifest as fault—whom does he not defile when situated nearby? (GāRaKō. 103)
Even through association with the virtuous, the impurity of the wicked does not indeed depart;
even when situated in the center of the lunar orb, the dark spot remains black.
O good man! Not even a trace of virtue has remained in you as you have been fashioned in this manner.
It is surely Fate itself that fashioned the wicked man in this world;
having seen his foul conduct, let the assembly revile him— it is not his fault.
A wicked person reviles even those of pure nature in their very presence. (GāRaKō.
106) Wherever a wicked person dwells, even while being nourished by affection and gifts, he defiles that very abode in no time, just like a lamp [soiling its stand]. (GāRaKō. 107)
One who is of low birth, double-tongued, yet sweet as long as food remains in the mouth—like a crow, such a wicked person cries out harshly once the meal is finished.
One who is devoid of virtue, lacking good qualities, and abandoned by the noble is born of the *loddha* tree. (GāRaKo. 108)
A slanderer pierces the heart of people like an arrow that has struck its mark.
He does not heed a request; who would not fear the wicked lion, whose mouth is agape even after devouring those who have fallen at his feet? (GāRakō. 109–110)
Behold the fruit obtained by abandoning the company of the wicked:
having reached the head of the Lord, it has acquired a fragrance as sweet as that of the *madanāhi* flower.

O friend, thinking "it will surely happen," one should [act] with the instruments of self-restraint within one's own mind. *GāRaKō* 111. *māmi* (O friend) is an address. *jantadiyaēhi* (with the instruments of life) refers to the senses.

Only the husks were released from the sesame seeds, while the kernels fell away through neglect. (GāRaKō.112) That sound, that whiteness, and even the birth of the conch in the ocean—all of it has vanished because of its heart’s crookedness. (GāRaKō.113)

Like clouds that have gathered rain, being exceedingly turbid and habituated to moving according to their own will, they distress the entire populace. (GāRaKo 14) The virtuous person labors in vain; it is only the wicked who truly captivate the hearts of lords.
A young man may cross by grasping fruits, but a five-faced one (Śiva) certainly cannot.
Now begins the section on a good master.]
Even for a lord of modest means, if his heart is pure, the great find favor;
even in a small mirror, great lords of elephants reflect themselves.
The grace of those possessing splendor, though slight, creates a vastness of majesty.
Even with a single ray of light, the moon traverses the sky. (GāRaKō.117) Even toward those naturally wicked who speak pleasant words, lords feel delight;
yet the arrow from the mouth of the crooked-hearted conch steals away the heart. (GāRaKō.118)
Even the rising sun does not destroy the mass of darkness situated below; or rather, those who remain loyal to their lord do not harm the host of enemies who have abandoned their pride. (GāRakō. 119)

Even when carried away by the powerful, particles of dust attain a high position; though they move upon the earth, they reach the sky through the wind. Likewise, those with masses of matted hair at their base and excellent foliage upon their heads [attain the highest state]. (GāRaKo 120)
If the Lord supports [the world] just as a tree does, then what is not sufficient? // GāRaKo.121 [14.
Now begins the section on Lakṣmī]
That which endures both new virtues and faults, and by whom even a single act of merit is embraced as the fortune of the world— salute that Blessed One,
Fortune (Lakṣmī). Even for those who are heavy with virtues, if they are devoid of wealth, their purposes do not come to fruition.
Even by means of a lamp, the day is not seen when there is separation from the sun.
(GāRaKō.123) Between Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī is heavy and Sarasvatī is light; otherwise, how could even those who have acquired knowledge follow after the Lord? (GāRaKō.124)
Fortune is invariably accompanied by virtues, yet virtues do not necessarily possess fortune;
indeed, lightning accompanies the clouds, but the clouds do not always possess lightning.
The moon, with its rays spreading coolness, has become full in its orb.
Thinking thus, Fortune dwells in him in every limb.
(GāRaKō.126) The root of Fortune’s nature is established in the world upon the foundation of virtue and power; for by their increase alone, she ascends upward. (GāRaKō.127)
[15. Now, the section on generosity:
Indeed, one who gives gives only the gift; he does not commit an act of contempt toward anyone.
The world does not bow even to elephants if they are devoid of giving.

(GāRaKo 128) Even while giving millions, those who bow down and hold their very lives for the sake of supplicants—how indeed could there be no twanging sound from such men, who are like bows? (GāRaKo 129)
This is indeed some unique quality of the bamboo: that even when the arrows have been released from the bowstring, they reach their target. (GāRakō.
Only for a single arrow does the twang of the bowstring at the moment of its beauty become fruitful;
he by whom a multitude of suitors was sent away after being bowed to becomes beloved to all the world, even though he gives only water—such a one is a fire. (Gāthākośa 131)
A friend causes distress even when his hand is constantly extended [in friendship].
(GāRakō 132) The wish-fulfilling trees give fruits as desired, yet they do not say anything at all;
having given water, the clouds thunder while their forms are wreathed in smoke. (GāRakō 133)

The hand of a giver attains greatness even when it has released its gift; yet, for those who do not give, it becomes a source of wonder and lightness, even if it is laden with gold. (GāRaKo 134) Neither the loss of a mate nor separation from his female elephant distresses the mind of an elephant as much as the bond [of attachment].

Just as when a swarm of bees is bewildered by the loss of their honey, he who endures hundreds of weapons in the midst of battle with the ease of a lotus stalk—truly, even his heart trembles at the moment of giving. (GāRaKō. 135–136)
Now begins the section on bad masters:
One who delights in the company of the dull-witted, who speaks with unpleasant words constantly, and who is ever...

Is the ocean one who has manifested many kinds of faults? No, for even a bad master [is like it]. (GāRaKō.137) When the great qualities have perished, even those of minor qualities become worthy of service;
when the sun has set, people long even for a lamp. (GāRaKō.138)
"O King, you have been caught by us in the Dharma; now, O performer, let us go!
No one has seen your gift, which is like that of a painted elephant.
(GāRaKo 139) "Whosoever are lords upon this earth, they are all like stalks of sugarcane."
Among the sapid and the insipid, inequalities are seen in their leaves.
(GāRaKō.140) Nowadays, the lords possess lordship; what [lordship] belongs to the ancient lords?
Faults and virtues were created by them through virtues and faults; indeed, they were not created by those [ancient lords]. (GāRaKō.141)

The lord turns his back and withdraws his own power from one who is self-reliant; the ocean does not obstruct the position of jewels above it, yet it does not provide them with its reflection. Thus, satisfaction arises in the mind of no one toward a group of servants who have fallen into misfortune. (GāRaKo 142)
The prosperity of the poor shines forth as if it were the prosperity of the Lord of Stars (the Moon);
let alone any other unprecedented wealth, even among the riches of the Lord of Stars.
Whatever ancient power of saving others may have existed, even that has been lost.
When the sun is happy, the lotuses are happy; when the sun is suffering, the lotuses suffer; yet nevertheless, the stain of the mud did not leave them because of that. (GāRaKō.145)
Just as the sun, as it reaches higher and higher altitudes,
becomes lighter and more intensely scorching, so too do some [people] become exceedingly firm.
That the power of the stars was destroyed by the powerful Lord of Stars (the Moon)— [this is the nature of the world].
Even the fortune of all the arts withers away because of him alone.
Even the goodness of one's attendants is of no avail when the master is treacherous;
even when the son of the Sun (Saturn) is unfavorable, other auspicious planets become fruitless.

May the venerable Vācakendras—Kīrtivijaya and Vijayagaṇi—who possess intense splendor and whose moon-like fame arises from the ocean of the universe, live long and forever! By serving the lotus-feet of those two venerable masters, who produced the sprout of wisdom as if by a spray of pure water, the humble and respectful Vinayavijaya has written this ocean of elegant sayings (*sūktārṇava*). This *Gāthāratnakōśa*, which resembles an unbroken necklace adorning the throat-pedestals of millions upon millions of Vācakas, is the supreme nectar. It was written by the Gaṇin Vinayavijaya, whose body is purified by the mass of pollen from the lotus-feet of the venerable Gaṇi Kīrtivijaya, who is the ornament of the throats of all the millions of Vācakas. *Śrīṁ!
